title: How Toy Testing Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore toy testing in two senses: market research testing where kids play with toys and are observed (including how to get toy-tester gigs through companies, blogs, YouTube), and safety testing by labs like Intertek and standards bodies (ASTM, EU rules, UK burn rate). They trace toy history from ancient toys through Enlightenment and industrialization, the dangerous toys of the mid-twentieth century (Empire Lady stove, Bird of Paradise slingshot, Zulu blowgun, lawn darts), the flammable fabrics act and pajama loophole, and modern dangerous toys (snacktime Cabbage Patch kid, Atomic Energy Lab, C.S.I. fingerprint kit with tremolite asbestos, Buckyballs magnets, Easy Bake Oven burns). They also discuss unboxing YouTube channels such as Disney Collector and Evan Tube HD. Ends with a listener mail about FOIA requests being used to stall research.

segments.title: Opening banter and toy testing anecdotes
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with Chuck's past product testing gigs (beer, frozen yogurt) and childhood wishes to be a toy tester, plus Josh's air guitar concerts. They note toy testing sounds fun for kids but tiring for parents.

segments.title: History of toys and play
segments.summary: Toys date back thousands of years, with Enlightenment thinkers in the eighteenth century promoting learning through play. Industrialization and mass production led to a consumer toy culture, especially in America in the 1950s.

segments.title: Dangerous vintage toys and injury statistics
segments.summary: Toy injury tracking was not done until recently; a 1968 estimate of 700,000 toy injuries is cited, and by 2012 eleven children had died, mostly from tricycles and scooters. The National Commission on Product Safety in the same era recommended bans on toys such as the Empire Lady stove, the Bird of Paradise slingshot, and the Zulu blowgun.

segments.title: Flammable Fabrics Act and pajama loophole
segments.summary: Flash fire deaths of children in rayon pajamas in the 1940s led Congress to pass the Flammable Fabrics Act. Flame retardant chemicals later raised concerns, and a mid-1990s loophole allowed snug-fitting pajamas without flame retardants. Chuck and Josh discuss the tobacco industry rumor and smoking in bed.

segments.title: Modern toy safety standards and testing labs
segments.summary: Toy safety rules are continually updated. ASTM created a standard consumer safety specification for toys. Testing companies such as Intertek test toys by biting, pulling, and burning them. The UK and EU set burn rate limits (about one inch per second, with warning labels in some ranges). Teddy bear seam strength testing is described.

segments.title: Market research toy testing and observation
segments.summary: Companies test toys by watching kids play to see if they are fun. Mattel's Imagination Center in El Segundo lets families with children aged zero to thirteen play with toys observed through two-way mirrors. Fisher-Price has a Play Lab.

segments.title: How to become a child toy tester
segments.summary: Ways to land toy-testing work include emailing companies with a resume and video of a child, auditioning, social media, mommy blogs receiving products, and kids' YouTube channels. Ellen DeGeneres featured kid toy testers, including Noah Ritter.
topics: how to become a toy tester

segments.title: Unboxing YouTube channels
segments.summary: Discussion of popular toy unboxing and review channels: Joe Randazzo's Lego Dude reviews, Evan Tube HD with millions of subscribers, and Disney Collector run by a Florida couple who earn large sums from unboxing videos.

segments.title: Infamous dangerous toys list
segments.summary: The hosts list infamous dangerous toys: the snacktime Cabbage Patch doll, which chewed anything placed in its mouth and was recalled by Mattel; lawn darts, banned in the US; the Atomic Energy Laboratory with real radioactive materials; the C.S.I. fingerprint kit containing tremolite asbestos; Buckyballs magnets that caused intestinal injuries and a lawsuit; and the Easy Bake Oven, which caused burns and a finger amputation.

segments.title: Listener mail on FOIA requests stalling research
segments.summary: A listener named Brandon points out that FOIA requests are being used by activist groups to stall legitimate research, a point missed in the Freedom of Information Act episode. The hosts thank him and give contact info.
